chapter_theme: Paripadal 3, to Tirumal: all classes of being spread out from the god, the Veda's praises of the bird, the boar and the swan, the uncounted hands and forms that only he can know, the lord of both gods and asuras for whom there is no enemy or friend, the god as the essence of each thing ruling the worlds with grace as umbrella and aram as sceptre, and a closing litany of names.

paripadal:3:1-14.reading: The poet hails the dark one whose flawless red feet cut off rebirth and says that the five elements, the sun and moon, aram, the sons of Diti and of Vidhi, the eight, the eleven, the two, Dharma, the lion and the three-times-seven worlds with all that lives in them have been told as things spread out from him, as the unfailing true word declares; the rare Veda of the brahmins pours forth that he is both the one born in the lotus and that one's father.
paripadal:3:1-14.nuance: The catalogue of lines 4 to 9 lists cosmic classes by number (the eight, the eleven, the two) without naming them, as a hearer who knew the list would supply them; the poet does not claim to see this himself but reports it as what the Veda says (lines 11 and 14), so the hymn's authority is borrowed from the brahmins' scripture. Line 5 differs strongly from sangamtamil.com's text.

words: மறு பிறப்பு அறுக்கும் மாசு இல் சேவடி
thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god as the source of all, sung as கடவுள் வாழ்த்து under paadaan

paripadal:3:15-30.reading: The poet gives the praises the gods sing: you are the bird that seized the nectar from the jewelled immortals and ended its mother's distress, lord of the tall banner of that bird; who does not worship your red feet, the foot that reached the seven lower worlds; when fire, death, Yama and the thousand-rayed sun gathered in the sea at the age's end you ploughed up the great earth with a boar's tusk, and when the waters of the sky dried you dried your wings as a swan; our song follows the way those singers sing.
paripadal:3:15-30.nuance: Lines 16 and 17 repeat the same half-line (பயந்தோள் இடுக்கண் களைந்த புள்ளின்), a chaining device that turns the bird first into the god himself and then into his banner. The boar and swan deeds are put in quotation as the gods' own hymn (எனவும் ... எனவும், lines 24, 26), and the poet then claims only to sing in their manner, so the human song is modelled on a heavenly one.

thinai_evidence.note: the god's deeds recited as worship: paadaan

paripadal:3:31-50.reading: Your forms and names differ, slayer in burning anger, and your hands take the shape of your fame: the one hand without fairness that mixed the nectar and swerved from even-handedness, then two hands, three, four and on through ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand and a hundred thousand, and more than these, a body whose count no number bounds; if one thinks of something like you, who but you could know it, first of the ancient word, whose beauty in learning, strength, mind and perception knows no limit?
paripadal:3:31-50.nuance: The first hand in the count is a reproach, not a praise: the hand that dealt out the nectar unfairly (lines 33 and 34) remembers the god's partiality to the gods against the asuras, which the next unit seems to answer by making him first of both. ஆம்பல் in line 44 is most likely the name of a very large number, not the water lily. The object of எரி சினம் கொன்றோய் (line 32) is missing; see source_issues.

thinai_evidence.note: praise by the uncountable forms of the god: paadaan

paripadal:3:51-62.reading: You are first of the immortals, who wear gem-set ornaments and feed on the moon of sixteen sweet rays as it waxes from crescent to full, and you are first also of the asuras who, when you strode across the earth, turned, fainted, fled and leapt into the sea in fear of you, their cool garlands loosening; so for those who know your nature, is there any sorting of these as enemies and those as friends? Rider of the bird that took the thousand-headed serpent in its beak, first of time whom they call red-eyed Maal, we know your nature from the way they cry out to you.
paripadal:3:51-62.nuance: The claim of line 58 is placed on the knower, not only on the god: it is those who know his nature (நின் மரபு அறிவோர்க்கே) who can no longer divide the world into his enemies and friends, though the same lines tell how the asuras fled from him in terror. Line 62 is hard to construe. Line 54 differs strongly from sangamtamil.com's text.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god as lord of gods and demons alike: paadaan

paripadal:3:63-80.reading: You are the burning in fire and the fragrance in the flower, the gem among stones and the truth in speech, the love in aram and the strength in valour, the secret of the Veda and the first of the elements, the light of the hot sun and the coolness of the moon; you are all things and the inner substance of all, so you have neither a dwelling nor a place to dwell; in the work of the first, middle and last orders there is no birth you have not taken and no one who gave you birth; with grace as your umbrella and aram as your sceptre you made the three-times-seven worlds a single shade with no second shade, and you are the one the count of the ages, void, quarter, half, one, two and on to nine, proclaims.
paripadal:3:63-80.nuance: The 'X in Y' series (lines 63 to 68) names in each pair the quality that makes a thing what it is, so the god is the essence, not the bulk, of each; this is why the poet can conclude that he has no dwelling place. Lines 71 and 72 hold both that he is born in every order and that no one bore him. இரு நிழல் படாமை (line 75) borrows the king's boast of a single umbrella with no rival over the land. The numbers of line 77 (பாழ், கால், பாகு) may be zero, a quarter and a half, or void and categories of a cosmology; the reading is not fixed.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god as the essence of all and the sovereign of the worlds: paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the god's grace as the shelter of the worlds
the god's aram as the rule of the worlds

paripadal:3:81-94.reading: The poem closes in a litany of names: red-eyed dark one, black-eyed white one, gold-eyed green one, green-eyed Maal, cowherd and guardian, unseen ancient, unforgetting mind, unfailing king who rules the world, poet of the old way, bard of the fine lute, lord of the garland, of the undefeated horn, of the gold-twisted garment and the colour of the right-whorled conch, wielder of the wheel, wrestler of fighting strength, husband of Tiru; and it ends on the lotus cup that, in the first time before the great earth took shape, bloomed in the midst of the fearful flood together with the son of the true word, the shade of your wheel.
paripadal:3:81-94.nuance: The names of lines 81 and 82 pair each eye with a body of another colour (red-eyed dark, black-eyed white, gold-eyed green, green-eyed Maal), giving the god several coloured forms at once, which echoes the difference of forms named in line 31. The last line ties the creation lotus that bore Brahma (line 93, cf. line 13) to the god's own wheel, but the syntax of line 94 is loose, and இடவல and குடஅல (line 83) are not clear.

thinai_evidence.note: the closing litany of the god's names: paadaan

links.note: Paripadal 2.16-17 names one age of creation after the boar form (கேழல் திகழ்வரக் கோலமொடு பெயரிய ஊழி); Paripadal 3.21-24 tells the deed itself, the god as a boar ploughing up the great earth with his tusk when fire, death and the sun gathered in the sea at the age's end.
links.teaches: Read together, the two hymns show the boar descent known in Sangam Vaishnava worship both as a label for a cosmic age and as a narrated rescue of the earth from the flood, so the avatar was already a deed that also served to count time.

links.note: Paripadal 1.32-39 says even sages free of delusion find the god hard to know and asks him to accept inadequate praise; Paripadal 3.45-47 asks whether anyone but the god himself could know what is like him (நின்னைப் புரை நினைப்பின் நீ அலது உணர்தியோ).
links.teaches: The first hymn stops at the limit of the praiser's knowledge, while the third turns that limit into a claim about the god, that he is the only knower of himself, so the pair shows the apology of the Tamil hymn hardening into a doctrine of self-knowledge.

links.note: Kural 4 names God as the one without liking or aversion (வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான்); Paripadal 3.53-58 makes Maal first of the immortals and first also of the asuras who fled from him into the sea, and asks whether there is any 'these are enemies, these friends' for those who know his nature.
links.teaches: The Kural states the god's freedom from liking and aversion as a bare attribute, while the hymn tests it against the war of gods and demons, where the god plainly took a side, and saves it by making him lord of both, so the pair shows the attribute had to be defended against a mythology of partisan war.

links.note: Purananuru 35.14-21 tells Killivalavan that his sky-touching umbrella is not to keep off the sun but to shelter suffering subjects, under a sceptre like aram itself; Paripadal 3.74-76 says the god, with grace as umbrella and aram as sceptre, made the twenty-one worlds a single shade with no second shade.
links.teaches: The puram poet has to argue the king into reading his umbrella as protection, a meaning the king may fail, whereas the hymn makes protection the umbrella's very substance in the god and takes over the royal boast of one shade with no rival, so the pair shows divine kingship and the counsel to kings using one ideal to measure each other.

links.note: Paripadal 3.63 says 'you are the fragrance in the flower' (பூவினுள் நாற்றம் நீ) in a run of identities; Tirumanthiram 2639 says the Lord is like the fragrance in the flower, the ghee in milk and the juice in fruit (பூவினுள் நாற்றமும் போலுளன்), mingled everywhere.
links.teaches: The same image of fragrance in the flower is an identity in the Sangam hymn, where the god is the essence of each thing, and a simile in Tirumular, where the Lord is like that essence and stands mingled in things, so the pair shows the later Saiva poet keeping the image while holding the god at one remove from the world he pervades.

source_issues: Paripadal 3: the colophon has no thinai or thurai; பாலையாழ் is the pan, a musical mode, not a thinai.

Paripadal 3 line 32: a line flagged as dropped for a modern heading (கூந்தல் என்னும் பெயரொடு கூந்தல்) reads as verse: it would supply the object of எரி சினம் கொன்றோய் (the slaying of the demon named for hair), so our text likely lacks a genuine line here; line 31 (வடிவு வேற்றுமையும் பெயர் வேற்றுமையும்) also reads like a heading but is kept as verse.
Paripadal 3 lines 5 and 54 differ strongly from sangamtamil.com (தாளும், தோளும், எருத்தொடு பெரியை; சூர் மருங்கு அறுத்த சுடர்ப் படையோயே); ours kept.
Paripadal 3 lines 16 and 17 repeat a half-line (பயந்தோள் இடுக்கண் களைந்த புள்ளி-); it reads as deliberate chaining, not a copying error.
Paripadal 3 lines 62, 77, 83 and 94 are hard to construe in our text.
